content.title: About
content.content: Creamed chipped or dried beef is finely ground beef that has been dried to a low moisture level and blended with a small amount of fat and spices, giving it a creamy texture and rich flavor. It is commonly used as a snack, an addition to salads, soups, and quick‑cook dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Drying meat has been a traditional method for armies to preserve food without refrigeration.
The creamy consistency is achieved by adding a modest amount of animal or vegetable fat and thorough mixing.
In many post‑Soviet countries the product is often called “beef jerky,” although jerky is usually drier and tougher.
The snack is high in protein and low in carbohydrates, making it popular among athletes and low‑carb dieters.
Low‑temperature drying retains most B‑vitamins that are naturally present in beef.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: A 30 g serving provides about 10 g of complete protein, essential for muscle repair and immune function.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: The product contains virtually no sugar, suitable for low‑carbohydrate diets.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune health and wound healing.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Especially vitamin B12, important for nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: To enhance flavor the product is often salted; high sodium intake can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: Preservatives and flavorings
items.content: Certain versions may contain additives that are unsuitable for people sensitive to food additives.

items.title: Possible nitrite use
items.content: Nitrites are sometimes used to preserve color; excess nitrites have been linked to increased cancer risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Creamed dried beef can be eaten straight from the pack, tossed into salads, soups, rice or noodle dishes, or used as a filling for sandwiches and wraps. Letting it reach room temperature before serving helps release its aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in an airtight package. For storage longer than three months, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation. Discard if it develops a sour smell or off‑color.

content.title: About
content.content: Ice cream cake is a dessert that combines layers of soft sponge cake soaked with ice cream and a creamy frosting. It often features multiple ice‑cream flavors, as well as fruit, nuts, or chocolate decorations. Served chilled, it is suitable for celebrations and everyday treats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first ice cream cake appeared in the United States in the early 20th century as an alternative to traditional butter cakes.
There are more than 30 popular flavor combinations, ranging from classic vanilla to exotic mango‑coconut.
Cakes are frequently adorned with edible flowers and gold leaf, making them popular at weddings.
In Russia, ice cream cake became widespread in the 2010s thanks to the growth of café‑dessert chains.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The dairy base of the ice cream provides calcium, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk and eggs used in the sponge are rich in vitamins B2 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: The custard frosting and dairy base supply a modest amount of protein for tissue repair.

items.title: Antioxidants from fruit layers
items.content: When berries or other fruits are added, they contribute antioxidants that help protect cells.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Ice cream contains lactose, so those with intolerance should choose lactose‑free versions.

items.title: Milk‑protein allergy
items.content: Casein and whey proteins can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The cake is often sweet, which may be problematic for people with diabetes or those watching weight.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of the creamy frosting and ice cream, a serving can exceed 400 kcal.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the cake into portions and serve immediately after removing from the freezer. Fresh berries, mint leaves, or grated chocolate can be added to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the ice cream cake in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Before serving, let it sit out for 10–15 minutes to make slicing easier. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 30 minutes, as it will melt.

content.title: About
content.content: Light Italian dressing is a blend of vegetable oils, vinegar, lemon juice, spices and herbs such as oregano, basil and garlic. It offers a bright aroma, moderate acidity and low calorie content, making it popular for salads and marinades.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Italian dressing originated in the United States in the early 20th century as an adaptation of traditional Mediterranean flavors.
The light version typically contains 30–40 % oil, with the remainder made up of vinegar, lemon juice and flavorings.
The herbs used in the dressing have antioxidant properties.
In the US the dressing is commonly sold in 250–500 ml bottles.
There are many variations, including mustard, honey or dried vegetable powders.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: Light dressing provides roughly 50–70 kcal per tablespoon, allowing generous use without significantly raising the energy content of meals.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Herbs and spices (oregano, basil, garlic) contain polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: When olive oil is part of the formula, the dressing can improve lipid profiles thanks to its monounsaturated fats.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Vinegar and lemon juice stimulate gastric juice production, enhancing nutrient absorption.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: The vegetable oils supply vitamin E, a potent antioxidant.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to mustard, garlic or specific oils.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Certain commercial versions contain higher levels of salt, which may be unsuitable for people with hypertension.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The high acidity of vinegar can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Commercial products may include preservatives such as potassium sorbate, which can cause sensitivity in some consumers.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Light Italian dressing can be tossed with green or vegetable salads, used as a marinade for chicken, fish or tofu, and added to roasted vegetables or pasta for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dressing in a tightly sealed bottle in the refrigerator. Once opened, it typically remains good for 2–3 months. Discard if the smell, color or taste changes.

quiche-with-meat-poultry-or-fish.title: Quiche with meat, poultry or fish

content.title: About
content.content: Quiche with meat, poultry or fish is an open pastry filled with an egg‑cream mixture and a chosen protein (beef, chicken, turkey, fish). The crust can be shortcrust, puff pastry or yeasted dough, and the filling is often enriched with vegetables, cheese and herbs. The dish is a staple of European cuisine and can be served hot or cold.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Quiche originated in medieval France and originally contained no eggs, only milk and cheese.
There are more than 30 regional quiche variations in France, each with its own set of fillings.
Traditional French quiche is often cut into triangular slices for serving.
Quiche can be baked in a conventional oven or microwaved, but only the oven creates a golden crust.
In the United States the classic “Quiche Lorraine” uses bacon and cheese without meat, poultry or fish.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Meat, poultry or fish provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and meat contain vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat and liver, often used in quiche, are good sources of easily absorbed iron.

items.title: Calcium from cream and cheese
items.content: The dairy components contribute calcium for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: Fish, especially fatty varieties, adds omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart and brain health.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Quiche contains cream, cheese and pastry, so portions should be moderate for weight management.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Dairy and meat can raise cholesterol levels if consumed excessively.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken, turkey or fish may harbor salmonella or listeria.

items.title: Allergy to eggs or dairy
items.content: People with egg or milk allergies should use alternative recipes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Quiche is served warm, slightly cooled, or completely cold. Cut into serving slices and pair with a green salad, fresh vegetables or a light vinaigrette. Mustard or tartar sauce can be added for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the baked quiche to room temperature, then cover with plastic wrap and refrigerate for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container – it keeps well for up to 2 months. Before reheating, ensure the interior reaches at least 75 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Summer squash (yellow or green) is a young, tender variety of zucchini harvested before full maturity. It has a soft texture, a mildly sweet flavor, and a bright color. It is commonly sautéed in a small amount of oil to retain its moisture and aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Summer squash belongs to the cucurbit family and is closely related to cucumbers and pumpkins.
The yellow and green types differ only in pigment; their nutritional profiles are virtually identical.
It is about 95 % water, making it very low in calories.
Easy to grow in greenhouses or open fields, it can be harvested in 50‑60 days.
Culinary uses include French‑style sauté, stews, casseroles, and gratins.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: One cup of sliced summer squash provides roughly 20 kcal, ideal for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports immune function and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Contains vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: Yellow squash is especially high in beta‑carotene, a provitamin A.

items.title: Good source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and blood pressure.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to cucurbit vegetables.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying non‑organic squash, rinse thoroughly to reduce pesticide exposure.

items.title: Excess sodium
items.content: Adding too much salt during cooking can offset the vegetable’s health benefits.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the squash into rounds or half‑moons and quickly sauté in vegetable oil until lightly golden. It can be added to salads, stews, pasta dishes, omelets, and casseroles. Serve the dish promptly to retain its crisp texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep summer squash in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, wrapped in a paper towel or a perforated bag. Stored properly, it stays fresh for 3‑5 days. Avoid storing it with ethylene‑producing fruits.
